newsitem.title: USA: Robust jobs data raise Fed specter, hit US markets.
newsitem.headline: Robust jobs data raise Fed specter, hit US markets.

text.p: A broadly robust U.S. employment report boosted estimates of fourth quarter economic growth on Friday, raising the specter of higher interest rates and jolting U.S. financial markets.

The jobs data, which came on the heels of a series of economic reports suggesting healthy growth, aggravated Treasury market concerns about already tight labor markets, sending the 30-year bond yield to three-month highs.
In the stock market, which cued off of bonds to open markedly lower, losses appeared to be better contained, with interest-rate sensitive issues taking the brunt of the damage.
Reassured by the limited stock retreat, the dollar cheered the strong payrolls numbers, hitting a 29-month high against the German mark and creeping higher versus the yen.

"It's a very solid report, the job gains are broad-based, and each of the components of the report look healthy and strong," said Michelle Colley Laughlin, Treasury market strategist at Prudential Securities Inc.
"It suggests Gross Domestic Product growth in the fourth quarter in excess of 3.0 percent, and it's likely to raise concerns that the Fed is going to be tightening," she added.

The report showed that a heady 262,000 jobs had been added to the U.S. economy in December, considerably more than the 192,000 predicted by Wall Street economists, and up from a revised 127,000 in November.
The key average hourly earnings and workweek components of the report, both used as gauges of labor market tightness, posted ample gains as well.

Earnings were up six cents or 0.5 percent, versus forecasts for a 0.2 percent rise, while the average workweek pushed up to 34.8 hours, substantially higher than the 34.5 hour week expected for the month.

"There was a real sharp rise in earnings ... and it's going to make the Federal Reserve nervous," said Ward McCarthy, managing director at Stone & McCarthy Research Associates Inc. "It's just going to resurrect concerns that labor market conditions are too tight."
While Treasuries cringed at the thought of higher rates, stocks and the dollar seemed to focus on the positive economic implications of the report.
